Class ItemSources

java.lang.Object
com.trevlar.slotkit.api.item.ItemSources
public final class ItemSources extends Object
Every item a player has, including the ones inside shulker boxes and bundles, to any depth: one walk, with every write going back up the chain of containers to the top-level slot. What to look for and what to do with it stay with the caller. 
// Take one totem from anywhere in scope, nearest first.
ItemStack used = ItemSources.take(player, scope, s -> s.has(DataComponents.DEATH_PROTECTION), 1);

// Visit everything; return false to stop.
ItemSources.walk(player, scope, ref -> { ...; return true; });

Order

Nearest first, level by level: the inventory's own slots (hotbar first), then every item one container deep in the inventory, then two deep; then each carried attachment (in declaration order), then the ender chest, each in the same order. Within one source a shallower item always comes before a deeper one.

Carried attachments

A player attachment declared playerAttached(...).carried() holds things the player carries (a pocket, a carried ender chest). Under ItemScope.carried its slots are walked like the inventory's, with source ItemRef.Source.CARRIED and paths naming the attachment. A client sees an attachment's contents when they reach it: through a menu holding its slots (the player's inventory menu, for a slot added there on both sides), or always for playerAttachedVisible.

Containers

A shulker box item's minecraft:container contents (written back with ItemContainerContents.fromItems, so empty slots keep their places) and a bundle's minecraft:bundle_contents (rebuilt in the same order; copyWithContents would reverse it). Other items with contents are not walked.

Open screens

A write sets a new component on the live top-level stack. Item-backed storage (StorageAttachment.itemContainer, and any storage that rereads when the component object changes) shows the change on its next read, so a screen showing the same shulker stays in step.

Other containers

The Container overloads of walk, find and at do the same from a container the caller supplies, such as the chest a player has open; their paths have source ItemRef.Source.CONTAINER. Ordering across sources is the caller's.

Menus on a nested item

live(ServerPlayer, ItemPath) binds a LiveItem to an item at a path, for a menu that stays open on it across many writes and closes when it goes stale.

Server side only, on the server thread, except find.

      public static net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack take(net.minecraft.server.level.ServerPlayer player, ItemScope scope, Predicate<net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack> test, int count)
      Takes count of the first item, nearest first, that test accepts. Returns what was taken, EMPTY if no item matched. Takes from one stack only.

    • find

      public static List<ItemSources.Found> find(net.minecraft.world.entity.player.Player player, ItemScope scope, Predicate<net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack> test)
      Every item in scope that test accepts, nearest first, read only: paths and copies, nothing written. Safe on either side. On the client it reads the contents that ride on the item stacks the client has. Vanilla never sends a client its ender chest's contents outside the chest's own menu, so a client finds nothing there; carried attachments are as the class notes say. A client sends a chosen ItemSources.Found.path() to the server, which acts on it with at(ServerPlayer, ItemPath).

    • at

      public static @Nullable ItemRef at(net.minecraft.server.level.ServerPlayer player, ItemPath path)
      The live item at path, or null when it isn't there: a slot out of range, an empty slot, an index past a container's contents, or a step through an item that isn't a shulker box or bundle. For acting on a path a client chose: the server checks the item is still what the client expects, then takes from it. The reference is as fresh as a walk's, so a take writes back up the chain.

    • pathOf

      public static @Nullable ItemPath pathOf(net.minecraft.world.entity.player.Player player, net.minecraft.world.inventory.Slot shown)
      The path of the item in a menu slot, for acting on a slot the player clicked: an inventory main slot, an ender chest slot, or a slot over one of this player's carried attachments. null for any other slot (armor, offhand, crafting, a chest).

      Either side, with the same answer for the same slot: a client drawing a slot names its item as the server will. A creative tab's slot names the slot it shows. On a client an ender chest's menu slots aren't the player's ender chest (vanilla gives the client a stand-in container), so there they are null: a mod that knows the ender chest is open names them itself. Since 2.2.0.

    • containerOf

      public static @Nullable net.minecraft.world.Container containerOf(net.minecraft.world.entity.player.Player player, ItemPath path)
      The player's container a path starts in: the inventory, the ender chest, or a carried attachment's contents. null for a supplied container's path, or an attachment that isn't carried. A carried attachment's container may be a new object on each call, but its stacks are the same objects as every other binding's (the menu's slots, a shift-click), until something changes them, so a stack can be tracked by identity from tick to tick. Since 2.2.0.

    • walk

      public static void walk(net.minecraft.world.Container container, ItemScope scope, ItemVisitor visitor)
      Visits each item in container and, with the scope's flags, the containers inside them, nearest first, until the visitor returns false. Every slot of the container is a top-level slot, in index order; the refs' source is ItemRef.Source.CONTAINER. The scope's enderChest flag doesn't apply. Server side only, on the server thread: pass the server's container (a chest's block entity, or the container behind its menu).

    • find

      public static List<ItemSources.Found> find(net.minecraft.world.Container container, ItemScope scope, Predicate<net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack> test)
      Every item in container that test accepts, as walk(Container, ItemScope, ItemVisitor) orders them, read only. Safe on either side: on the client, pass the container behind the open screen's menu, which the server keeps in step. Paths have source ItemRef.Source.CONTAINER and name the container's own slot index; the server resolves one with at(Container, ItemPath).

    • at

      public static @Nullable ItemRef at(net.minecraft.world.Container container, ItemPath path)
      The live item at a ItemRef.Source.CONTAINER path in container, or null when it isn't there (as at(ServerPlayer, ItemPath)) or the path's source is another one. The caller supplies the container the path was found in, typically the one behind the menu the player has open, so a client can't point the server at a container of its choosing.
